    <p class="result">TCP detection: Cascade Mask R-CNN, AP50 69.9 ± 0.6, single
    class. For reference, Mask R-CNN detection of Arctic ice-wedge polygons, the
    same landform produced by the same process on Earth, reports mAP 0.695 at IoU
    0.50 on matched-resolution aerial imagery (Zhang et al., 2018), on a task that
    also assigns polygon subtype and with training data several orders of magnitude
    larger than what exists for Mars.</p>

    <p class="caveat">The classification method and pilot deployment are under
    review at JGR: Machine Learning and Computation, submitted April 2026, not yet
    accepted. Detection metrics are from the planet-scale deployment in
    preparation. Train and test splits for the detector are made at the tile level,
    so adjacent tiles from the same image can appear in both; reported detection
    metrics should be read as an upper bound on generalization to unseen scenes.</p>

    <span class="entry-label">Results in preparation</span>
    <h3>Training on Earth, deploying on Mars</h3>
    <p>Can an AI vision model trained only on orbital Earth images identify similar
    landforms on Mars? Geologists have reasoned by terrestrial analogy for decades;
    this asks whether the analogy survives being made computational. I trained
    segmentation models on three Earth landform classes, arctic tundra polygons and
    two classes of desert channel network [REPLACE: name the two], and evaluated them
    on Mars orbital imagery, asking where the analogy held and what, if anything,
    still had to come from Mars.</p>

    <p>The analogy carried real signal for some landforms and hit a resolution floor
    for others. That boundary is the useful part of the result: it says which
    terrestrial training data is worth collecting for a given target and which is not.
    REPLACE: name which landforms fell on which side, and the one design decision a
    reviewer would question.</p>

    <img src="images/REPLACE-transfer.png" alt="REPLACE">

    <p class="result">Quantitative results withheld pending publication. For scale
    of the problem: on Earth alone, detection AP for this landform class falls from
    0.73 to 0.25 across cross-sensor transfer scenarios (Zhang et al., 2020). The
    Earth-to-Mars gap spans planet, sensor, and resolution at once.</p>

    <p class="links">
      <a href="https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2026/pdf/1717.pdf">LPSC 2026 abstract 1717</a>
      <span>Code not yet released</span>

  <div class="entry">
    <span class="entry-label">In preparation</span>
    <h3>Knowing what a record cannot tell you</h3>
    <p>REPLACE: two to four sentences. Determining whether the modern Mars dust
    storm catalog can support forecasting at all, before a forecaster is built.
    Name the union-find collapse from 26 major events to 13 independent episodes
    as the contested design choice, and say why it is defensible.</p>

    <img src="images/predictability-budget.png" alt="Predictability budget in units of sigma">

    <p class="result">For this record and design, detecting a precursor at 80%
    power requires roughly 1.7 to 1.8σ. The largest season-controlled effect
    measured is 0.32σ, one-sided 95% upper limit 0.80σ. Closing that gap by
    observation would take at least 150 Mars years; the modern record spans
    about 8.</p>

    <p class="caveat">This is a predictability assessment and not a forecasting
    system. Every floor statement is scoped to its design. The nulls exclude
    effects large enough to support prediction for the features and estimands
    tested; they are not evidence that precursors do not exist.</p>

    <p class="links"><span>Pre-registration and code: Zenodo deposit forthcoming</span></p>
  </div>

  <div class="entry">
    <span class="entry-label">In progress</span>
    <h3>Infrastructure for imagery at planet scale</h3>
    <p>Processing an orbital archive means not downloading it. I replaced a
    full-image decode subprocess with windowed Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF reads,
    verified by a parity test proving identical output before the change shipped,
    and built a client against NASA's PDS STAC API to discover HiRISE footprints
    programmatically. The pipeline runs on AWS Batch GPU Spot fleets, packaged in a
    multi-stage Docker build that separates CUDA compile and runtime images, with a
    kill switch so an unattended run cannot burn budget. GCP Vertex AI is
    configured as a second deployment target.</p>

    <p class="links"><span>Code released with the pipeline</span></p>
  </div>
